forest.title: System Design
forest.summary: Learn the building blocks first, then study how they interact in real systems.

children.title: Load Balancers
children.summary: A load balancer routes incoming requests across servers so none gets overloaded; it runs no app logic itself. Needed because horizontal scaling requires something to pick a server for each request.

children.title: Caching
children.summary: Storing the result of an expensive operation so repeated requests are answered fast.

children.title: Frontend System Design
children.summary: Frontend has its own scaling concerns: bundle size, rendering strategy, real-time updates via WebSockets, and micro-frontends.

angles.title: The Restaurant Analogy That Finally Made Load Balancers Click
angles.hook: I asked twice why a load balancer was needed and still didn't get it. Then it was compared to a restaurant host who seats people and cooks nothing. That clicked.

angles.title: I Used to Think Frontend Didn't Need System Design
angles.hook: I thought system design was only a backend thing. It isn't. Frontend has its own scaling problems, and I didn't know about them.

angles.title: How Load Balancers Work
angles.hook: Why one big server isn't enough, and what decides where requests go.

angles.title: What Frontend System Design Actually Covers
angles.hook: Bundle size, rendering, real-time updates and micro-frontends. The four areas it covers, in plain terms.
